The couple say they will learn the sex at birth. PEOPLE spells her late sister's name 'Kristen'; her own post (S02) spells it 'Kristin'.

claims.claim: The emphasis of her border story has shifted between tellings. The scripted 2016 video opens on a year in Mexico writing about brutality against women and turns on a bedridden resident of a border old folks' home asking whether the coverage meant help was coming; the 2017 interview names trafficking, drug smuggling and elderly people left at the border in one answer; the 2026 versions lead with cartel violence. claims.passage: told that I wasn't a team player because I never joined the happy hours.

claims.alternative: Told eighteen years later to a magazine during a book launch; uncorroborated. The 2017 interview's unnamed firm resembles Vanguard, so the two may be one episode (C120).

claims.passage: I am never going to let somebody hold me back because of my bank account.
claims.inference: A vow about never being subject to gatekeepers, which favors the control reading.
claims.alternative: Told eighteen years later during a book launch; uncorroborated.

claims.claim: In 2017 she told this story about an unnamed early employer: she proposed an international arm, was told she might run it, and hours later lost the job to someone else because, in her words, 'everyone thought I would leave dead bodies behind me to get whatever I wanted.'
claims.passage: I was told that everyone thought I would leave dead bodies behind me to get whatever I wanted.

claims.alternative: One telling, eight years old, of an unnamed employer and an unnamed boss; no other party has spoken. The firm's details resemble her accounts of Vanguard (C120). She had situational reasons to adapt as a junior employee who was often the only Latina in the group (C04, C117).

claims.claim: Asked whether the boss had really said that, she answered: 'Yep. And maybe he was right. It was a big realization for me. I thought that I was driven, but I was putting a different message out.'

claims.alternative: One answer in an advice interview, where presenting a lesson learned is the expected register, given while she was already promoting a personal brand (C119).

claims.claim: Her response, in her words: 'I became more aware of how people perceive me. I adapted. And then I just worked hard. I refused to let up.' She adds that the woman who got the job later joined her team.

claims.inference: She changed how she came across and also did not let up. The edited article quotes the whole answer and no longer reads the last sentence as keeping a tally.

claims.claim: The lesson she drew: 'I think it's about personal brand.'

claims.inference: She generalized the episode into managing perception.
claims.alternative: In the same answer she ties it to standing out as Latinos and says 'Don't hide it, but be aware' (C117), so the lesson is partly about bias she faced. The article now reports that.

claims.claim: Told that colleagues saw her as ruthless, she refused the decision and accepted the perception; years later she still granted the verdict and had made a method of it, which suggests she treats a bad reputation as a fault in her own presentation.
claims.passage: That suggests a person who treats a bad reputation as a fault in her own presentation.
claims.inference: The article's reading of C09, C58, C59 and C116, marked with 'suggests' and said to lean toward Three without settling it.
claims.alternative: One telling from 2017 of an unnamed boss; no other party has spoken. A pragmatic Eight could adapt tactically, and a junior Latina employee had career reasons to adapt whatever her type; the article states both.

claims.alternative: Disowning borrowed ambitions is a popular creator narrative and she teaches 'mimetic desire' as a concept. Retrospective.

claims.passage: being in the marriage was part of my identity and I didn't know how to let go of it and I felt like I was failing and there was massive shame and guilt around it

claims.alternative: Her former husband is a private person who has not spoken; the draft confines itself to her statements about her own experience, names no one and adds no detail. The quotation is from unpunctuated lowercase captions of a 2022 clip; the draft capitalizes 'I' and changes nothing else. A further characterization of that marriage in the same clip is deliberately not used.

claims.claim: In an interview published September 21, 2026 she said she went to a bank to borrow against a business and was told the account she believed held about a million dollars was nearly empty; she quotes herself asking to see the screen.
claims.passage: "Excuse me, can you please turn that thing around so I can see what's on that screen?"

claims.passage: If you haven't sat in the dark in the middle of the night with no idea of what to do next, you're not really in the game.
claims.inference: The father as the person she calls in a crisis. Her site attributes a differently worded version of the line to him, which the article now says.
claims.alternative: His words reach us only through her.

claims.claim: She describes the pain of that episode as 'my identity and that I was a failure because I had let an entire business fail'.
claims.passage: Like just my identity and that I was a failure because I had let an entire business fail.
claims.inference: The wound she names is failure and identity. She says she went to the head of operations (C110), blamed herself (C78) and built a tracking system. This is the 2026, on-message instance of a pattern with earlier instances (C15, C16).
claims.alternative: The business is unnamed and undated and the story is uncorroborated. It was told three days after the book's release in answer to a question about the book, so it serves the campaign. Owners are trained to say 'it was my fault'.

claims.claim: Of the manager who she says hid the shortfall: 'it was my fault for not tracking him, obviously.'
claims.passage: it was my fault for not tracking him, obviously.
claims.inference: Let down by a subordinate, she says she went to him (C110) and then blamed herself. The article counts this as granting the judgment, not as never confronting anyone.
claims.alternative: Owners are trained to say 'it was my fault', and in the same telling her father's advice is not to hunt for the culprit. The manager is unnamed and has not given an account.

claims.claim: A little over twenty minutes after the bank story in the same interview, asked for her real dream, she said her vision changes over a career and that 'at first, early on for me' it was: 'I don't ever want anybody to have control over me or my life again.'
claims.passage: I don't ever want anybody to have control over me or my life again.

claims.alternative: One answer in one interview, reconstructed years later. 'Prove yourself' is the host's phrase. The sentence serves the book's title. Her next sentence ties 'again' to employers (C80).

claims.claim: She added 'I'll become every single thing that you said I wouldn't' and 'I was angry'; when Lewis Howes said 'You were trying to prove yourself', she answered 'Oh, yeah.'
claims.passage: "I'll become every single thing that you said I wouldn't,"
claims.inference: Anger as fuel favors Type 8; becoming what doubters said she could not, and proving herself, is achievement as vindication.
claims.alternative: 'Prove yourself' is the host's phrase. The quoted sentences are separated by others in the source and the draft presents them separately.

claims.claim: Immediately after 'again' she says what she means: 'I don't ever want to have to work for somebody I don't like or to spend a moment of my day in somebody else's life architecting their dream instead of mine.'
claims.passage: I don't ever want to have to work for somebody I don't like or to spend a moment of my day in somebody else's life architecting their dream instead of mine.
claims.inference: Her own continuation explains the word 'again': the control she means is working for employers. The draft's statement that she had not said who controlled her was wrong and is corrected.
claims.alternative: One answer in a campaign interview, from auto-captions (S11, about 1:09:22-1:09:53) not confirmed by ear.

claims.claim: In 2023 she defined being rich as 'having no master. That's what rich looks like for me.'
claims.passage: having no master. That's what rich looks like for me.
claims.inference: Autonomy language three years before the 2026 statement in C28, so the theme is not new to the book. The second half is about standing and being sought out, and about not being seen to want it.
claims.alternative: The 'club' lines are an argument for content marketing. 'Thirsty' is a concern about how one appears, which fits Three better than Eight.

claims.claim: In 2024 she called herself 'really intense' and 'kind of hard to work for sometimes'.
claims.passage: "really intense" and "kind of hard to work for sometimes"
claims.inference: Self-labels of intensity that support the Type 8 alternative.
claims.alternative: Unpunctuated captions; said while arguing that admitting flaws protects against being cancelled, which is itself image management.

claims.claim: No statement by her of an Enneagram type was found, and no credible published typing of her.
claims.passage: As of October 2026, no statement by her of her own type has been found.
claims.inference: The type on the page is this site's interpretation and should be presented as such. Her remark is a joke about a different system and settles nothing.
claims.alternative: A self-typing may exist in an interview this run did not read; absence of a found statement is not proof there is none.
claims.review_trigger: Before each release, search for any statement by her about her Enneagram type; if one exists, report it and weigh it.

claims.claim: She said in 2026 that a fan telling her she is cool is 'totally uninteresting to me', whereas someone who bought a business because of her 'did something'.
claims.passage: totally uninteresting to me,
claims.inference: The contrast she draws is flattery against results she caused. The edited article moves the line out of the Type 8 case and uses it, with its contrast, where the Three reading is tested.
claims.alternative: It cuts both ways: it disclaims admiration, and it measures her effect by other people's visible results.

claims.claim: She describes her marriage as a mutual defense pact: 'our thing is it's us against the world'.
claims.passage: our thing is it's us against the world
claims.inference: Her account of how she behaves with the person closest to her: dominant at work, yielding at home, and accepting correction from him. The us-against-the-world frame favors the Eight alternative; taking feedback as a practice favors neither strongly.
claims.alternative: Public descriptions of a marriage by one spouse, three years apart. Petkas's only on-record remarks found are on her podcast and are about fitness (S17).

claims.claim: She told Entrepreneur she does not want to be on social media every day, 'But it serves my goal'.
claims.passage: Do I really want to be on social media every day? No. But it serves my goal,
claims.inference: She presents visibility and scale as instruments chosen for a goal, at a cost she says she does not enjoy. Fits a goal-driven reading and complicates any claim that she seeks attention for its own sake.
claims.alternative: A person with an audience in the millions calling herself a reluctant influencer should be read skeptically.

claims.claim: Her statements of anger, autonomy, toughness and marriage-as-alliance make a genuine case for Type 8.
claims.passage: that is a real Eight case
claims.inference: The article's statement of the strongest alternative, built from C28, C80, C79, C29, C70, C83 and C27, with her responses to being told no (C135) added.
claims.alternative: Every element is self-described and several coincide with her brand.

claims.claim: Applying the test to every setback the article narrates: where a gatekeeper held her back (Vanguard in the 2026 telling, First Trust) she names control; where the judgment was on her or nobody stood in the way (the dead-bodies verdict, the marriage, Mount Baker, the emptied account) she names how she came across or failing. Infertility is not counted.
claims.passage: What she says was damaged depends on the setback.
claims.inference: The corrected first half of the discriminator. It replaces the draft's claim that five tellings uniformly named failure and that she never confronted anyone.
claims.alternative: Every episode is self-told. The split may reflect the kind of story as much as the person: a gatekeeper story invites control language and a solo failure invites failure language.

claims.claim: In 2023 she said 'I don't ever want to be the person standing in line at the club. I want to own the club.'
claims.passage: I don't ever want to be the person standing in line at the club. I want to own the club.

claims.claim: Five of the tellings the article narrates involve a person who judged, blocked or failed her. In two (the Vanguard promotion in the 2026 telling and the Goldman trip) she concedes nothing. In three she contested the outcome and still conceded something, a different thing each time: to the 2017 boss a verdict on how she came across ('maybe he was right'); to First Trust's owners in 2023 the right to set the rules ('as is fair'); in the 2026 telling her own blame for not tracking the manager ('it was my fault').

Only the 2017 one is a judgment on her that she accepted. The mountain and the marriage are excluded as having no adversary.

If the 2017 and 2026 passed-over stories are one episode (C120), the same event is told once with a concession and once without. Later tellings of the First Trust exit repeat the concession and are not used in the article: 'I was total victim mindset about it' and 'he did me a huge favor by pushing me out' in 2024 (S08, 1:41:25-1:42:59), and 'That's all actually fair. They did me a giant favor' in 2026 (S03).

claims.claim: The article gives more weight to statements that predate the 2026 campaign: on the control side 'I just never accept the word no' (2017) and 'having no master' (2023); on the other 'maybe he was right' (2017), the marriage as 'part of my identity' (2022) and the Mount Baker story (told in 2023). Type 3 leads on a verdict on her image accepted and made into a method, a self-description as fearful, and the statement that she spent most of her life pleasing people.

claims.inference: The restated discriminator, now written as prose with each statement dated by when she said it. Both strands are old; the lead rests on what the second holds that an Eight seldom volunteers, which the article labels a judgment about how the types tend to talk.
claims.alternative: The 2017 and 2023 statements were also made by someone promoting herself, so 'pre-campaign' is not 'pre-incentive'. No outside testimony tests either strand.

type_hypothesis.against: Her most direct statement of motive is about control, not admiration: 'I don't ever want anybody to have control over me or my life again', with anger as the fuel (C28, C79), explained in her next sentence as never working for someone she does not like (C80). It has precedents in 2017 ('I just never accept the word no', C10), 2023 ('having no master', C29; 'it wasn't my casino', C12) and 2024 ('because I had ownership', C70). In every telling where a superior blocks her she refuses, goes around or leaves (C116, C118, C115, C135), which is what an Eight does. In the Vanguard telling the injury she names is being held back (C11, C57). She describes money as protection from other people's will (C07). She walked away from a prestige track into laundromats and car washes, says a 'managing director' tombstone does not interest her (C132), calls daily visibility a chore (C32) and a fan's praise uninteresting (C85). A Three is expected to move toward what earns admiration; she describes moving away from it (C134). Most of the Three evidence is retrospective storytelling by a professional communicator, her 2026 failure confessions serve the 2026 book as much as her control statements serve the brand (C92), and no one who has worked for or against her has been found on record (C102, C43).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 8 fits a real pattern. Across a decade she frames her life as a refusal to be controlled: she left journalism for 'the centers of power' (C06, C52), treats money as what decides 'who had protection' (C07), argued with the people who ran the business she built at First Trust and left when it 'wasn't my casino' (C12, C115), stayed under two years at most jobs until she had a stake (C70), and sells a pledge that reads 'I will not do what I am told' (C50). Told 'you can't', she got the idea approved elsewhere (C116); denied travel by a boss, she paid her own way (C118). She was told colleagues thought she would 'leave dead bodies behind' her (C09), calls herself 'really intense' and 'kind of hard to work for sometimes' (C83) and describes her marriage as 'us against the world' (C27). Her self-sufficiency ('the one who handles it, who doesn't need help', C24) is how Eights describe vulnerability. Type 6 was also considered: she names fear, de-risks carefully, calls her father in two crises and took her move into finance from a mentor (C13, C77, C52). It is set aside, less firmly than Eight is tested, because on Mount Baker she says the danger was not the frightening part and names failing in front of others (C15), and because what she says finance cost her was a borrowed measure of success, not safety (C14, C71); the article names Six and gives that reason (C129). Type 7 is unlikely given her stated indifference to fun in S11.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What she says was injured when a setback or a hostile judgment landed, and what she did next, scored separately. The second half does not separate the types: when a person stood in her way she mostly refused, went around or left (C135), which leans Eight. The first half splits by the kind of setback. Held back by a gatekeeper (Vanguard in the 2026 telling, First Trust) she names control (C57, C12). When the judgment was on her, or nobody stood in the way, she names how she came across or failing: 'I was putting a different message out' (C58), 'I felt like I was failing' (C16), 'am I like a failure' (C15), 'I was a failure' (C18). Five of the tellings the article narrates involve a person who judged, blocked or failed her. In two (the Vanguard promotion in the 2026 telling, the Goldman trip) she concedes nothing (C11, C57, C118). In three she contested the outcome and still conceded something, a different thing each time: a verdict on how she came across ('maybe he was right', the 2017 boss), the owners' right to set the rules ('as is fair', First Trust in 2023), and her own blame for not tracking a manager ('it was my fault', the 2026 telling) (C136). Only the first is a judgment on her that she accepted. The mountain and the marriage have no adversary and cannot test confrontation; infertility is not counted. One discount applies to both sides: control statements match the product and 2026 failure statements match the 2026 book (C92), so weight goes to what predates the campaign (C137). There, Type 3 leads on three things an Eight seldom volunteers: a verdict on her image that she accepted, still endorsed years later and turned into a theory of advancement ('personal brand', 'known and wanted'; C58, C60, C62), while already building a public persona as a finance employee (C119); a self-description as fearful and hedging ('scaredy-cat', 'wuss'; C13, C75); and the statement that she spent most of her life pleasing people toward goals she did not care about and 'chasing somebody else' (C72, C14). This is a judgment about how the types tend to talk, which is why confidence stays at medium. Limit: every episode is self-told. The reading should be reversed if people who have worked for or against her describe habitual open confrontation and indifference to how she is seen (research task 2).
type_hypothesis.unexplained: Why a person organized around achievement and image chose a deliberately unglamorous field, disowns the 'managing director' title and says the visible part of her work is a chore (C132, C32); the Three reading can call 'boring' a differentiated brand and results-caused a new scoreboard, but that is convenient (C134). The moral motive of her first career and the purpose she has stated since 2017, which fit either type and are not used to separate them (C56, C122, C111, C147). How she actually treats subordinates: her own accounts alternate between persuasion and being 'hard to work for' (C83), and no one else has spoken. Whether the confessional register of 2026 (infertility, fear, the empty bank account) is a change in her or in what her market rewards. Whether the 2017 and 2026 passed-over stories are one episode (C120). And her own open question: she says she does not know what she will want after the baby arrives (C101), and answered it with a plan to keep her options open (C143).
